title: Senior's toolkit: tracking, saving and conflicts
summary: See what SaveChanges will do, update in bulk without loading, handle concurrency conflicts and use transactions with cancellation.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: tracking, saving and conflicts
steps.body: Saving is where data gets lost: a silent overwrite, an update that loaded 100,000 rows, a half-finished transfer. These are the APIs experienced developers use to see, control and protect what gets written.

toolkit.what: One line per tracked entity with its key and state. Print it right before `SaveChanges` to see what will be sent.
flags: plus every property, with modified ones marked

toolkit.what: Read or set the state of one entity, and look at its original and current values.
flags: what was loaded against what you have now

toolkit.what: One UPDATE or DELETE statement for every matching row, without loading them. The tracker does not see these changes.
flags: the column and its new value; chain for more columns
no `SaveChanges` needed, and it ignores tracked entities

toolkit.what: Optimistic concurrency. The UPDATE includes the original token in its WHERE; if someone else changed the row, zero rows match and EF Core throws instead of overwriting their work.
flags: SQL Server `rowversion`, set by the database on every write
any property you change yourself, such as a `Version` number

toolkit.what: Someone changed or deleted the row since you read it. Reload and retry, or tell the user, usually with HTTP 409 or 412.
flags: what is in the database now (null if deleted)
accept their version as the new baseline, then retry

toolkit.what: Group several `SaveChanges` calls (or a save plus an `ExecuteUpdate`) so they all commit or none do. A single `SaveChanges` is already one transaction.
flags: rolls back automatically if you never commit
pass the request's CancellationToken to every async call

steps.prompt: Two support agents edit the same ticket. Agent A saves, then agent B saves, and A's change is gone. No error was logged. What fixes this?
options: Add a concurrency token (`IsConcurrencyToken()` or a `rowversion`), then catch `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` and return 409 so B reloads
steps.explain: Without a token, the UPDATE matches by id alone, so the last writer wins silently. With a token, B's UPDATE says `WHERE Id = 7 AND Version = 3`, finds no row and throws. A transaction does not help: each save was already atomic.

steps.prompt: A nightly job that marks old carts as abandoned takes 40 minutes and uses 6 GB of memory.
code: foreach (var c in carts) c.Status = CartStatus.Abandoned;
options: Replace it with `ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.Status, CartStatus.Abandoned), ct)`: one UPDATE, nothing loaded
steps.explain: The loop loads and tracks every row, then sends one UPDATE per row. `ExecuteUpdateAsync` sends a single `UPDATE ... WHERE UpdatedAt < @cutoff`. `AsNoTracking` would make it worse: nothing would be saved at all.

steps.prompt: Delete expired sessions in one statement and log how many went.
Match each API to what it tells you or does.
pairs: every tracked entity and its state
the values as they were loaded
someone changed the row since you read it
one UPDATE with no entities loaded
several saves commit together or not at all

steps.prompt: Which way of writing fits the job?
items: Change one order's address from a form
Rename a product, with a concurrency check
Add a line to an order, with validation in the entity
Purge 2 million log rows older than 90 days
Raise every price in a category by 5%
steps.explain: Single-entity edits want the tracker: validation, concurrency tokens, related entities. Set-based changes over many rows want one statement.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Give every entity that two people can edit a concurrency token, and decide what the user sees on a conflict. Use `ExecuteUpdateAsync` for anything that touches many rows, and pass the request's `CancellationToken` to every `SaveChangesAsync` and `ToListAsync`.
